references.authors: Walton RG, Dungan CM, Long DE, et al.
references.title: Metformin blunts muscle hypertrophy in response to progressive resistance exercise training in older adults: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial: The MASTERS trial.
references.finding: MASTERS: metformin 1700 mg/day during 14 weeks of progressive resistance training blunted gains in lean body mass and thigh muscle area versus placebo, with a non-significant trend to smaller strength gains.

references.authors: Konopka AR, Laurin JL, Schoenberg HM, et al.
references.title: Metformin inhibits mitochondrial adaptations to aerobic exercise training in older adults.
references.finding: Metformin (vs placebo) during 12 weeks of aerobic training attenuated the training-induced rise in whole-body insulin sensitivity and VO2max and abolished the rise in muscle mitochondrial respiration; responses were highly variable.

references.authors: Malin SK, Gerber R, Chipkin SR, et al.
references.title: Independent and combined effects of exercise training and metformin on insulin sensitivity in individuals with prediabetes.
references.finding: Exercise, metformin (2000 mg/day) and both combined all raised clamp insulin sensitivity over 12 weeks; the rise was 25-30% higher with exercise alone than with exercise plus metformin, a non-significant difference read as possible blunting.

references.authors: Boulé NG, Robert C, Bell GJ, et al.
references.title: Metformin and exercise in type 2 diabetes: examining treatment modality interactions.
references.finding: Metformin raised exercise heart rate and lactate; adding exercise reduced metformin's lowering of the post-meal glucose response (interaction P=0.05).

references.authors: Boulé NG, Kenny GP, Larose J, et al.
references.title: Does metformin modify the effect on glycaemic control of aerobic exercise, resistance exercise or both?
references.finding: Over 22 weeks of aerobic, resistance or combined training, background metformin use did not significantly change the training effects on HbA1c, fitness, strength or body weight.

references.authors: Pilmark NS, Lyngbæk M, Oberholzer L, et al.
references.title: The interaction between metformin and physical activity on postprandial glucose and glucose kinetics: a randomised, clinical trial.
references.finding: Metformin 2 g/day plus 12 weeks of interval cycling was not better than training alone for post-meal glucose; VO2peak rose 15% with no between-group difference.

references.authors: Moreno-Cabañas A, Morales-Palomo F, Alvarez-Jimenez L, et al.
references.title: Effects of chronic metformin treatment on training adaptations in men and women with hyperglycemia: A prospective study.
references.finding: Among people doing 16 weeks of HIIT, those already taking metformin gained about half as much VO2max (12.7% vs 25.3%) as non-users, although insulin-resistance improvements were similar.

references.authors: Etayo-Urtasun P, Sáez de Asteasu ML, Izquierdo M
references.title: The effects of metformin and exercise training on cardiorespiratory, blood pressure, and metabolic adaptations across the spectrum of glucose dysregulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Adding metformin to structured exercise modestly attenuated VO2peak gains (MD -1.19 mL/kg/min) and blood-pressure reductions, with no difference in weight, glycemic or lipid outcomes (moderate certainty for VO2peak).

references.authors: Grammer EE, Stahl ME, Ortiz de Zevallos J, et al.
references.title: Influence of metformin on exercise metabolism and capacity: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Metformin raised blood lactate during exercise (SMD 0.98) and modulated exercise metabolism; effects on exercise capacity depended on dose, duration and population.

references.authors: Kulkarni AS, Peck BD, Walton RG, et al.
references.title: Metformin alters skeletal muscle transcriptome adaptations to resistance training in older adults.
references.finding: Metformin dampened the muscle gene-expression response to resistance training while shifting some aging-related pathways (senescence, autophagy) in a possibly favourable direction.

references.authors: Terada T, Boulé NG
references.title: Does metformin therapy influence the effects of intensive lifestyle intervention? Exploring the interaction between first line therapies in the Look AHEAD trial.
references.finding: Background metformin was associated with slightly smaller weight loss (-4.7 vs -5.7 kg) under intensive lifestyle intervention and added little glycemic benefit, but did not change fitness gains.

references.authors: Barzilai N, Crandall JP, Kritchevsky SB, et al.
references.title: Metformin as a Tool to Target Aging.
references.finding: Rationale paper for TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin), proposing metformin as a first test of a drug targeting aging itself, based largely on observational data in diabetes.

references.authors: Konopka AR, Miller BF
references.title: Taming expectations of metformin as a treatment to extend healthspan.
references.finding: Argues that TAME goals may not match healthspan goals: metformin's benefits are documented in people with chronic disease, and whether they extend to healthy people (and alongside exercise) is unknown.

references.authors: Bannister CA, Holden SE, Jenkins-Jones S, et al.
references.title: Can people with type 2 diabetes live longer than those without? A comparison of mortality in people initiated with metformin or sulphonylurea monotherapy and matched, non-diabetic controls.
references.n: 78,241 metformin users, 12,222 sulphonylurea users, 90,463 matched controls
references.finding: In UK primary-care data, people with type 2 diabetes started on metformin had 15% longer adjusted survival than matched non-diabetic controls; this finding underpins much of the anti-aging interest in metformin.

references.authors: Keys MT, Thinggaard M, Larsen LA, et al.
references.title: Reassessing the evidence of a survival advantage in Type 2 diabetes treated with metformin compared with controls without diabetes: a retrospective cohort study.
references.n: Danish national registers incl. discordant twins
references.finding: Reanalysis using Danish registers and discordant twins found metformin-treated type 2 diabetes was associated with higher, not lower, mortality than no diabetes (adjusted IRR 1.32 singletons, 1.64 twins), contradicting Bannister 2014.

references.authors: Aroda VR, Edelstein SL, Goldberg RB, et al.
references.title: Long-term Metformin Use and Vitamin B12 Deficiency in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study.
references.finding: Metformin 850 mg twice daily was associated with more low or borderline B12 (<=298 pg/mL: 19.1% vs 9.5% at 5 years); each year of use raised deficiency odds 13%, and neuropathy was more common in metformin users with low B12.

references.authors: de Jager J, Kooy A, Lehert P, et al.
references.title: Long term treatment with metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes and risk of vitamin B-12 deficiency: randomised placebo controlled trial.
references.finding: Metformin 850 mg three times daily for 4.3 years lowered B12 by 19% versus placebo and raised absolute B12-deficiency risk by 7.2 percentage points (number needed to harm ~14), with higher homocysteine.

references.authors: Chapman LE, Darling AL, Brown JE
references.title: Association between metformin and vitamin B12 deficiency in patients with type 2 diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Metformin lowered vitamin B12 by about 57 pmol/L within 6 weeks to 3 months in pooled trials, pushing some patients into deficiency or borderline status.

references.authors: Rena G, Hardie DG, Pearson ER
references.title: The mechanisms of action of metformin.
references.finding: Metformin acts through AMPK-dependent and independent routes, including inhibition of mitochondrial respiration (complex I) and possibly mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase, with a growing role for the gut.

references.authors: Owen MR, Doran E, Halestrap AP
references.title: Evidence that metformin exerts its anti-diabetic effects through inhibition of complex 1 of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
references.finding: Metformin slowly accumulates in mitochondria and inhibits respiratory-chain complex I in hepatoma cells and rat liver, which restrains gluconeogenesis.

references.authors: Cameron AR, Morrison VL, Levin D, et al.
references.title: Anti-Inflammatory Effects of Metformin Irrespective of Diabetes Status.
references.n: cell, cohort and a nondiabetic heart-failure RCT
references.finding: Metformin suppressed NF-kB-linked inflammatory signalling in cells, lowered the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio versus sulfonylurea in a diabetes cohort, and reduced plasma cytokines in nondiabetic heart failure.

references.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.
references.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome.
references.finding: 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline (endorsed by ASRM, ESHRE, Endocrine Society, ESE): 254 recommendations including letrozole as first-line ovulation induction, metformin for metabolic features, and anti-obesity medicines alongside lifestyle.

references.authors: Sharpe A, Morley LC, Tang T, et al.
references.title: Metformin for ovulation induction (excluding gonadotrophins) in women with polycystic ovary syndrome.
references.finding: Cochrane: in PCOS, metformin may improve live birth versus placebo (OR 1.59, low quality) but quadruples GI side effects; adding it to clomiphene has uncertain effect on live birth; clomiphene beats metformin in obese women.

references.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. Electronic address: ASRM@asrm.org, Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
references.title: Role of metformin for ovulation induction in infertile patients with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): a guideline.
references.finding: ASRM: metformin raises ovulation versus placebo in PCOS but should not be first-line for anovulation because clomiphene or letrozole are much more effective; no added miscarriage when stopped at conception.

references.authors: Wensink MJ, Lu Y, Tian L, et al.
references.title: Preconception Antidiabetic Drugs in Men and Birth Defects in Offspring : A Nationwide Cohort Study.
references.finding: Offspring of fathers who filled metformin prescriptions during sperm development had more major birth defects (aOR 1.40), especially genital defects in boys; exposure outside that window showed no excess.

references.authors: Meng LC, van Gelder MMHJ, Chuang HM, et al.
references.title: Paternal metformin use and risk of congenital malformations in offspring in Norway and Taiwan: population based, cross national cohort study.
references.finding: After restricting to fathers with type 2 diabetes and adjusting for diabetes severity, paternal metformin during sperm development was not linked to malformations (pooled RR 0.89, 0.77-1.03), including in sibling comparisons.

references.authors: Bosman E, Esterhuizen AD, Rodrigues FA, et al.
references.title: Effect of metformin therapy and dietary supplements on semen parameters in hyperinsulinaemic males.
references.finding: Uncontrolled study: 3 months of metformin (with or without supplements) raised normal sperm forms from about 4% to 5.5% and improved chromatin packaging in hyperinsulinaemic men.

references.authors: Miller BF, Thyfault JP
references.title: Exercise-Pharmacology Interactions: Metformin, Statins, and Healthspan.
references.finding: Reviews how metformin and statins may blunt exercise adaptations and argues their healthspan use in disease-free people must be tested alongside exercise.

references.authors: Wilding JPH, Batterham RL, Calanna S, et al.
references.title: Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults with Overweight or Obesity.
references.finding: Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly plus lifestyle cut body weight 14.9% vs 2.4% with placebo over 68 weeks.

references.authors: Rubino D, Abrahamsson N, Davies M, et al.
references.title: Effect of Continued Weekly Subcutaneous Semaglutide vs Placebo on Weight Loss Maintenance in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: The STEP 4 Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: After a 20-week semaglutide run-in (-10.6%), continuing semaglutide lost a further 7.9% by week 68 whereas switching to placebo regained 6.9%.

references.authors: Jastreboff AM, Aronne LJ, Ahmad NN, et al.
references.title: Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity.
references.finding: Tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg weekly cut body weight 15.0%, 19.5% and 20.9% vs 3.1% with placebo over 72 weeks.

references.authors: Bray JJH, Foster-Davies H, Salem A, et al.
references.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve biomarkers of inflammation and oxidative stress: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
references.finding: GLP-1 receptor agonists lowered CRP (-0.54 mg/L), TNF-alpha and malondialdehyde (SMD -0.84) and raised adiponectin versus standard therapy or placebo; CRP fall tracked blood-pressure and insulin-resistance improvement.

references.authors: Kanbay M, Shah E, AlShiab R, et al.
references.title: Effects of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Inflammatory and Metabolic Biomarkers in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Incretin therapies lowered CRP (SMD -0.37) and MDA (SMD -0.98, only 3 trials) and raised adiponectin; IL-6 and TNF-alpha effects were not significant overall.

references.authors: Neeland IJ, Linge J, Birkenfeld AL
references.title: Changes in lean body mass with glucagon-like peptide-1-based therapies and mitigation strategies.
references.finding: Lean-mass loss on GLP-1 therapies is largely proportional to weight lost and may be adaptive (less muscle fat, better insulin sensitivity), but older or frail patients risk sarcopenia.

references.authors: Eisa N, Barood O
references.title: Lean Mass Changes With Incretin Therapy Versus Lifestyle Intervention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Lean mass made up 25-39% of weight lost on incretin drugs (semaglutide 35%, tirzepatide 25%), similar to diet-based weight loss (26%); adding resistance training cut it to about 17.5%.

references.authors: Batsis JA, Gavras A, Gross DC, et al.
references.title: Effect of Incretin-Based and Nonpharmacologic Weight Loss on Body Composition : A Systematic Review.
references.finding: Systematic review: loss of muscle-related indices exceeded prespecified benchmarks in about two thirds of incretin interventions and nearly half of non-drug weight-loss interventions.

references.authors: Forslund M, Wändell P, Forsberg L, et al.
references.title: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment in women with polycystic ovary syndrome-a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Meta-analysis informing the PCOS guideline: GLP-1 agonists as add-on lowered BMI by 1.38 kg/m2 (low certainty); evidence on reproductive, metabolic and psychological outcomes remains insufficient.

references.authors: Han Y, Li Y, He B
references.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists versus metformin in PCOS: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Versus metformin, GLP-1 agonists improved insulin sensitivity and lowered BMI and waist more in PCOS, with more nausea; evidence moderate to low.

references.authors: Salamun V, Jensterle M, Janez A, et al.
references.title: Liraglutide increases IVF pregnancy rates in obese PCOS women with poor response to first-line reproductive treatments: a pilot randomized study.
references.finding: Pilot open-label trial: 12 weeks of liraglutide 1.2 mg plus metformin before IVF (with a 4-week washout) gave higher pregnancy rate per transfer (85.7% vs 28.6%) than metformin alone despite similar weight loss.

references.authors: Skelley JW, Swearengin K, York AL, et al.
references.title: The impact of tirzepatide and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists on oral hormonal contraception.
references.finding: Tirzepatide significantly reduced oral-contraceptive exposure (AUC, Cmax) via delayed gastric emptying, whereas studies of other GLP-1 agonists showed no clinically significant effect.

references.authors: Dilbaz B, Ateş Ç
references.title: The effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists on fertility, contraception, and pregnancy: clinical perspectives.
references.journal: Eur J Contracept Reprod Health Care
references.finding: GLP-1 agonists help obesity-related infertility (notably PCOS); clinicians should counsel on contraceptive reliability, ensure washout before conception and note limited pregnancy-safety data.

references.authors: Cesta CE, Rotem R, Bateman BT, et al.
references.title: Safety of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Other Second-Line Antidiabetics in Early Pregnancy.
references.n: 51,826 infants of mothers with type 2 diabetes (Nordic, US, Israel)
references.finding: First-trimester GLP-1 agonist exposure was not associated with more major congenital malformations than insulin (adjusted RR 0.95, 0.72-1.26).

references.authors: Hviid KVR, Banasik K, Mortensen LH, et al.
references.title: Periconceptional GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure and obstetric outcomes: a Danish nationwide cohort study.
references.finding: Periconceptional liraglutide or semaglutide was linked to preterm birth only in women with diabetes (aOR ~1.7-1.8), not in those using them for weight management, pointing to the underlying diabetes.

references.authors: Ozbek L, Shah E, Al-Shiab R, et al.
references.title: Safety of GLP-1 and Dual GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonists in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Lactation: A Systematic Review of Maternal, Fetal, and Neonatal Outcomes.
references.finding: Periconceptional or early-pregnancy GLP-1-based therapy was not consistently linked to malformations, growth restriction, stillbirth or neonatal death; data on continued use through pregnancy are limited.

references.authors: Drummond RF, Seif KE, Reece EA
references.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use in pregnancy: a review.
references.finding: AJOG review: malformation data lack glycemic-control information, so periconceptional safety cannot be concluded; recommends contraception for all patients on GLP-1 agonists.

references.authors: Andersen E, Juhl CR, Kjøller ET, et al.
references.title: Sperm count is increased by diet-induced weight loss and maintained by exercise or GLP-1 analogue treatment: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: An 8-week low-calorie diet (-16.5 kg) raised sperm concentration 1.49-fold and count 1.41-fold; the gain was kept at 52 weeks in men who maintained weight loss (including with liraglutide or exercise) but lost in those who regained.

references.authors: Gregorič N, Šikonja J, Janež A, et al.
references.title: Semaglutide improved sperm morphology in obese men with type 2 diabetes mellitus and functional hypogonadism.
references.n: obese men with type 2 diabetes and functional hypogonadism
references.finding: Semaglutide raised normal sperm morphology (median 2% to 4%) and testosterone, whereas testosterone therapy lowered sperm concentration and count.

references.authors: Deameh MG, Ramez M, Rowaiee R, et al.
references.title: Effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists on male reproductive hormones, semen parameters, and metabolic outcomes: a systematic review.
references.finding: GLP-1 agonists consistently raised total testosterone in men with obesity or type 2 diabetes while preserving LH/FSH; semen improvements were reported in obese or hypogonadal men but not in healthy men.

references.authors: Peel A, Lyons H, Tully CA, et al.
references.title: The effect of obesity interventions on male fertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Lifestyle weight-loss interventions modestly improved sperm morphology and progressive motility in men; data on GLP-1 agonists and on conception outcomes were too limited to judge.

references.authors: Oesterle A, Laufs U, Liao JK
references.title: Pleiotropic Effects of Statins on the Cardiovascular System.
references.finding: Statins block isoprenoid synthesis and thereby Rho/Rac signalling and NADPH oxidase activity, lowering ROS and inflammation in cells and animals; how much this adds clinically beyond LDL lowering is debated.

references.authors: Ridker PM, Danielson E, Fonseca FA, et al.
references.title: Rosuvastatin to prevent vascular events in men and women with elevated C-reactive protein.
references.n: 17,802 adults with LDL <130 mg/dL and hsCRP >=2 mg/L (JUPITER)
references.finding: Rosuvastatin 20 mg cut LDL 50% and hsCRP 37% and nearly halved major cardiovascular events (HR 0.56), with more physician-reported diabetes.

references.authors: De Caterina R, Cipollone F, Filardo FP, et al.
references.title: Low-density lipoprotein level reduction by the 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme-A inhibitor simvastatin is accompanied by a related reduction of F2-isoprostane formation in hypercholesterolemic subjects: no further effect of vitamin E.
references.finding: Simvastatin's LDL lowering was accompanied by a proportional fall in urinary F2-isoprostanes; adding vitamin E 600 mg/day did not lower lipid peroxidation further.

references.authors: Singh U, Devaraj S, Jialal I, et al.
references.title: Comparison effect of atorvastatin (10 versus 80 mg) on biomarkers of inflammation and oxidative stress in subjects with metabolic syndrome.
references.finding: Atorvastatin 80 mg cut oxidized LDL 39% (vs 24% with 10 mg) and lowered hsCRP and NF-kB activity over 12 weeks.

references.authors: Banach M, Serban C, Sahebkar A, et al.
references.title: Effects of coenzyme Q10 on statin-induced myopathy: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: CoQ10 supplementation did not significantly reduce statin-associated muscle pain (SMD -0.53, CI -1.33 to 0.28) or CK.

references.authors: Qu H, Guo M, Chai H, et al.
references.title: Effects of Coenzyme Q10 on Statin-Induced Myopathy: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: CoQ10 reduced statin-associated muscle pain, weakness, cramps and tiredness versus placebo, without changing CK.

references.authors: Taylor BA, Lorson L, White CM, et al.
references.title: A randomized trial of coenzyme Q10 in patients with confirmed statin myopathy.
references.n: 120 patients with reported statin myalgia; 41 randomized to CoQ10 or placebo
references.finding: Only 36% of people reporting statin myalgia had symptoms on blinded simvastatin vs placebo; ubiquinol CoQ10 600 mg/day raised serum CoQ10 fourfold but did not reduce pain.

references.authors: Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration
references.title: Effect of statin therapy on muscle symptoms: an individual participant data meta-analysis of large-scale, randomised, double-blind trials.
references.finding: Statins caused a 7% relative excess of muscle pain or weakness in year 1 (about 11 per 1000 person-years); only about 1 in 15 muscle complaints on statins was actually due to the drug.

references.authors: Mikus CR, Boyle LJ, Borengasser SJ, et al.
references.title: Simvastatin impairs exercise training adaptations.
references.finding: Simvastatin 40 mg blunted the training-induced gain in cardiorespiratory fitness (1.5% vs 10%) and turned a 13% rise in muscle citrate synthase into a 4.5% fall over 12 weeks.

references.authors: Kokkinos PF, Faselis C, Myers J, et al.
references.title: Interactive effects of fitness and statin treatment on mortality risk in veterans with dyslipidaemia: a cohort study.
references.finding: Statin use and higher fitness were independently associated with lower mortality, and the combination (highly fit statin users HR 0.30) was lowest of all.

references.authors: Panza GA, Taylor BA, Thompson PD, et al.
references.title: The Effect of Atorvastatin on Habitual Physical Activity among Healthy Adults.
references.finding: Atorvastatin 80 mg for 6 months did not reduce habitual physical activity differently from placebo.

references.authors: Chang JC, Chen YJ, Chen IC, et al.
references.title: Perinatal Outcomes After Statin Exposure During Pregnancy.
references.finding: Statin use in pregnancy was not associated with congenital anomalies but was associated with low birth weight (RR 1.51) and preterm birth (RR 1.99).

references.authors: Bateman BT, Hernandez-Diaz S, Fischer MA, et al.
references.title: Statins and congenital malformations: cohort study.
references.finding: First-trimester statin use showed no teratogenic effect after adjustment for confounders such as diabetes (RR 1.07, 0.85-1.37).

references.authors: Vahedian-Azimi A, Makvandi S, Banach M, et al.
references.title: Fetal toxicity associated with statins: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Statin use in pregnancy was not significantly associated with birth defects (OR 1.48, 0.90-2.42), though the authors call for more data.

references.authors: Dutta D, Mahajan K, Jena S, et al.
references.title: Feto-maternal safety of statins in pregnancy: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Statins in pregnancy were not associated with congenital malformations (OR 1.05); low birth weight signals were confined to non-pravastatin use in cohort studies.

references.authors: Anagnostis P, Papanikolaou D, Ioannidou PG, et al.
references.title: The effect of statins on semen parameters in patients with hypercholesterolemia: A systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review of pravastatin and simvastatin found no consistent harmful effect on semen volume or concentration, with mixed motility and morphology findings.

references.authors: Keihani S, Martin C, Craig JR, et al.
references.title: Semen parameters are unaffected by statin use in men evaluated for infertility.
references.n: 118 statin users vs 7698 unmedicated subfertile men
references.finding: Statin use for over 3 months was not associated with changes in semen parameters other than a small fall in volume in combination users.

references.authors: Pons-Rejraji H, Brugnon F, Sion B, et al.
references.title: Evaluation of atorvastatin efficacy and toxicity on spermatozoa, accessory glands and gonadal hormones of healthy men: a pilot prospective clinical trial.
references.finding: Atorvastatin 10 mg for 5 months was followed by a 31% fall in total sperm count and changes in accessory-gland markers, some persisting 3 months after stopping.

references.authors: Peters AL, Buschur EO, Buse JB, et al.
references.title: Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis: A Potential Complication of Treatment With Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibition.
references.finding: Case series establishing euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitors; normal glucose delayed recognition.

references.authors: Mistry S, Eschler DC
references.title: Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis Caused by SGLT2 Inhibitors and a Ketogenic Diet: A Case Series and Review of Literature.
references.finding: Euglycemic DKA occurred with an SGLT2 inhibitor after only one week of a ketogenic diet; patients on these drugs should avoid ketogenic diets.

references.authors: Cowie MR, Fisher M
references.title: SGLT2 inhibitors: mechanisms of cardiovascular benefit beyond glycaemic control.
references.finding: Proposed SGLT2-inhibitor benefit mechanisms include natriuresis, ketone use, reduced inflammation and oxidative stress and less AGE signalling; mostly from mechanistic work.

references.authors: Lauterburg BH, Mitchell JR
references.title: Therapeutic doses of acetaminophen stimulate the turnover of cysteine and glutathione in man.
references.finding: Single therapeutic doses of acetaminophen (600-1200 mg) markedly increased turnover of the cysteine pool used for glutathione synthesis, showing that normal doses draw on glutathione.

references.authors: Watkins PB, Kaplowitz N, Slattery JT, et al.
references.title: Aminotransferase elevations in healthy adults receiving 4 grams of acetaminophen daily: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Starting 4 g/day acetaminophen produced ALT >3x the upper limit in 31-44% of healthy adults within 2 weeks versus 0% on placebo.

references.authors: Bauer AZ, Swan SH, Kriebel D, et al.
references.title: Paracetamol use during pregnancy - a call for precautionary action.
references.finding: Consensus statement by 91 scientists calling for precaution: pregnant women should use acetaminophen only when indicated, at the lowest dose for the shortest time, citing neurodevelopmental and urogenital associations.

references.authors: Alwan S, Conover EA, Harris-Sagaribay L, et al.
references.title: Paracetamol use in pregnancy - caution over causal inference from available data.
references.finding: Letter from teratology and pharmacoepidemiology experts cautioning against causal inference from the observational acetaminophen-pregnancy data.

references.authors: Ahlqvist VH, Sjöqvist H, Dalman C, et al.
references.title: Acetaminophen Use During Pregnancy and Children's Risk of Autism, ADHD, and Intellectual Disability.
references.finding: Small associations of prenatal acetaminophen with autism (HR 1.05) and ADHD (HR 1.07) disappeared in sibling comparisons (HR 0.98 for both), suggesting familial confounding.

references.authors: Prada D, Ritz B, Bauer AZ, et al.
references.title: Evaluation of the evidence on acetaminophen use and neurodevelopmental disorders using the Navigation Guide methodology.
references.finding: Navigation Guide review: 27 of 46 studies reported positive associations of prenatal acetaminophen with ADHD/autism, with higher-quality studies more often positive; authors urge limiting use.

references.authors: Kristensen DM, Hass U, Lesné L, et al.
references.title: Intrauterine exposure to mild analgesics is a risk factor for development of male reproductive disorders in human and rat.
references.n: Danish and Finnish birth cohorts plus rat studies
references.finding: Mild analgesic use in pregnancy (especially second trimester) was dose-dependently linked to cryptorchidism in the Danish but not the Finnish cohort; paracetamol was anti-androgenic in rats.

references.authors: Smarr MM, Grantz KL, Sundaram R, et al.
references.title: Urinary paracetamol and time-to-pregnancy.
references.finding: Men in the highest quartile of urinary paracetamol had longer time to pregnancy (fecundability OR 0.67); no association when modelled continuously or in women.

references.authors: Trappe TA, Carroll CC, Dickinson JM, et al.
references.title: Influence of acetaminophen and ibuprofen on skeletal muscle adaptations to resistance exercise in older adults.
references.journal: Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol
references.finding: Over-the-counter doses of acetaminophen (4 g/day) or ibuprofen (1.2 g/day) during 12 weeks of resistance training did not inhibit muscle growth and strength and appeared to enhance them (muscle volume +12.5% and +10.9% vs +8.6% on placebo) in older adults.

references.authors: Lilja M, Mandić M, Apró W, et al.
references.title: High doses of anti-inflammatory drugs compromise muscle strength and hypertrophic adaptations to resistance training in young adults.
references.finding: Ibuprofen 1200 mg/day halved quadriceps growth (3.7% vs 7.5%) in young men and women and blunted strength gains versus low-dose aspirin during 8 weeks of resistance training.

references.authors: Lundberg TR, Howatson G
references.title: Analgesic and anti-inflammatory drugs in sports: Implications for exercise performance and training adaptations.
references.finding: NSAIDs and paracetamol inhibit COX; NSAIDs interfere with hypertrophy and strength gains in young people, while effects in elite athletes are unproven.

references.authors: Schoenfeld BJ
references.title: The use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for exercise-induced muscle damage: implications for skeletal muscle development.
references.finding: Occasional NSAID use is unlikely to impair muscle growth; chronic use is less clear and may be detrimental in people with high growth potential.

references.authors: Kristensen DM, Desdoits-Lethimonier C, Mackey AL, et al.
references.title: Ibuprofen alters human testicular physiology to produce a state of compensated hypogonadism.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.n: young healthy men plus human testis explants
references.finding: Daily ibuprofen in young men lowered the testosterone/LH ratio, producing compensated hypogonadism, and suppressed testosterone production in human testis explants.

references.authors: Micu MC, Micu R, Ostensen M
references.title: Luteinized unruptured follicle syndrome increased by inactive disease and selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors in women with inflammatory arthropathies.
references.n: 59 monitored cycles with NSAIDs vs untreated cycles in women with inflammatory arthritis
references.finding: Continuous periovulatory NSAIDs caused luteinized unruptured follicle in 35.6% of cycles vs 3.4% untreated; etoricoxib was the main culprit and ibuprofen 1600 mg/day caused none.

references.authors: Smith G, Roberts R, Hall C, et al.
references.title: Reversible ovulatory failure associated with the development of luteinized unruptured follicles in women with inflammatory arthritis taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
references.finding: Three women with inflammatory arthritis had recurrent luteinized unruptured follicles on NSAIDs, with normal ovulation after stopping.

references.authors: Stone S, Khamashta MA, Nelson-Piercy C
references.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and reversible female infertility: is there a link?
references.finding: COX-2 inhibition blocks follicle rupture; animal data and three small clinical studies link regular NSAIDs to reversible anovulation, so withdrawal should be considered during fertility work-up.

references.authors: Li DK, Ferber JR, Odouli R, et al.
references.title: Use of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs during pregnancy and the risk of miscarriage.
references.finding: NSAID use around conception was associated with more miscarriage (aHR 1.89), stronger for early loss and longer use; acetaminophen users were used as an indication control.

references.authors: Chen X, Yang Y, Chen L, et al.
references.title: Pregnancy outcomes and birth defects in offspring following Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs exposure during pregnancy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Early-pregnancy NSAID exposure was associated with more congenital anomalies (OR 1.28) and major birth defects (OR 1.19); miscarriage association was not significant (OR 1.20).

references.authors: Tanrikut C, Feldman AS, Altemus M, et al.
references.title: Adverse effect of paroxetine on sperm.
references.finding: Five weeks of paroxetine raised mean sperm DNA fragmentation from 13.8% to 30.3% (TUNEL); abnormal fragmentation rose from 9.7% to 50% of men (OR 9.3) without changes in standard semen parameters.

references.authors: Koyuncu H, Serefoglu EC, Yencilek E, et al.
references.title: Escitalopram treatment for premature ejaculation has a negative effect on semen parameters.
references.finding: Escitalopram 10 mg daily for 12 weeks lowered sperm concentration, motility and morphology.

references.authors: Akasheh G, Sirati L, Noshad Kamran AR, et al.
references.title: Comparison of the effect of sertraline with behavioral therapy on semen parameters in men with primary premature ejaculation.
references.finding: Sertraline 50 mg/day for 3 months (vs behavioural therapy) lowered sperm concentration and normal morphology and raised sperm DNA fragmentation.

references.authors: Safarinejad MR
references.title: Sperm DNA damage and semen quality impairment after treatment with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors detected using semen analysis and sperm chromatin structure assay.
references.finding: Reported lower sperm count and motility and higher DNA denaturation with SSRIs; the journal issued an Expression of Concern in 2023, so this paper should not be relied on.

references.authors: Beeder LA, Samplaski MK
references.title: Effect of antidepressant medications on semen parameters and male fertility.
references.finding: SSRIs, especially fluoxetine, are linked to lower sperm concentration and motility and higher DNA fragmentation in human and animal studies; effects appear reversible; data on other antidepressants are sparse.

references.authors: Sylvester C, Menke M, Gopalan P
references.title: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors and Fertility: Considerations for Couples Trying to Conceive.
references.finding: Insufficient evidence that SSRIs reduce female fertility or IVF outcomes; six of seven mostly poor-quality male studies found adverse effects on semen.

references.authors: Nillni YI, Wesselink AK, Gradus JL, et al.
references.title: Depression, anxiety, and psychotropic medication use and fecundability.
references.finding: Severe depressive symptoms lowered fecundability (FR 0.62) regardless of treatment; psychotropic medication use itself did not appear to harm fecundability.

references.authors: Casilla-Lennon MM, Meltzer-Brody S, Steiner AZ
references.title: The effect of antidepressants on fertility.
references.finding: Cycle-specific antidepressant use was associated with lower fecundability (FR 0.75, CI crossing 1; 0.66 after adjusting for depression history), with confounding by depression unresolved.

references.authors: Evans-Hoeker EA, Eisenberg E, Diamond MP, et al.
references.title: Major depression, antidepressant use, and male and female fertility.
references.n: 1650 women and 1608 men in infertility trials
references.finding: Active major depression in the male partner lowered conception; maternal antidepressant use (n=90) was associated with first-trimester pregnancy loss.

references.authors: Yland JJ, McKinnon CJ, Hatch EE, et al.
references.title: A Prospective Study of Male Depression, Psychotropic Medication Use, and Fecundability.
references.finding: Male depression history was weakly associated with lower fecundability (FR 0.89, CI crossing 1); current psychotropic medication use statistically mediated 44% of the depressive-symptom association.

references.authors: Anonymous
references.title: Treatment and Management of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 5.
references.finding: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 5 on treating perinatal depression and anxiety, supporting SSRIs as first-line pharmacotherapy and individualized decisions rather than stopping effective treatment.

references.authors: Amory JK, Wang C, Swerdloff RS, et al.
references.title: The effect of 5alpha-reductase inhibition with dutasteride and finasteride on semen parameters and serum hormones in healthy men.
references.finding: Dutasteride 0.5 mg and finasteride 5 mg cut total sperm count by 28.6% and 34.3% at 26 weeks, lowered volume and motility, with largely reversible effects after stopping.

references.authors: Overstreet JW, Fuh VL, Gould J, et al.
references.title: Chronic treatment with finasteride daily does not affect spermatogenesis or semen production in young men.
references.finding: Finasteride 1 mg daily for 48 weeks did not affect sperm concentration, count, motility or morphology versus placebo.

references.authors: Samplaski MK, Lo K, Grober E, et al.
references.title: Finasteride use in the male infertility population: effects on semen and hormone parameters.
references.finding: In men presenting with infertility while on finasteride (mean 1 mg/day), sperm counts rose on average 11.6-fold after stopping; 57% of severely oligospermic men rose above 15 million/mL.

references.authors: Bawor M, Bami H, Dennis BB, et al.
references.title: Testosterone suppression in opioid users: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Regular opioid use (including methadone) lowered testosterone in men by about 165 ng/dL versus controls; no effect seen in women.

references.authors: Drobnis EZ, Nangia AK
references.title: Pain Medications and Male Reproduction.
references.finding: Exogenous opioids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and act directly on the testis, lowering semen quality and raising DNA fragmentation; NSAIDs have less effect; paracetamol may be of concern.

references.authors: Toovey S, Hudson E, Hendry WF, et al.
references.title: Sulphasalazine and male infertility: reversibility and possible mechanism.
references.finding: Sulphasalazine 2-4 g/day caused gross semen abnormalities in 18 men treated over 2 months; quality recovered after withdrawal and 10 pregnancies followed.

references.authors: O'Moráin C, Smethurst P, Doré CJ, et al.
references.title: Reversible male infertility due to sulphasalazine: studies in man and rat.
references.n: men with IBD plus rat studies
references.finding: Sulphasalazine caused oligospermia, poor motility and abnormal forms that reversed on withdrawal (15 pregnancies at a median 2.5 months); the sulphapyridine moiety was responsible in rats.

references.authors: Eck LK, Jensen TB, Mastrogiannis D, et al.
references.title: Risk of Adverse Pregnancy Outcome After Paternal Exposure to Methotrexate Within 90 Days Before Pregnancy.
references.finding: Paternal methotrexate within 90 days before conception was not associated with major malformations (aOR 1.01), stillbirth or preterm birth.

references.authors: Perez-Garcia LF, Röder E, Krijthe BP, et al.
references.title: Is methotrexate safe for men with an immune-mediated inflammatory disease and an active desire to become a father? Results of a prospective cohort study (iFAME-MTX).
references.finding: Semen parameters and sperm DNA fragmentation did not change after starting low-dose methotrexate and matched healthy controls; methotrexate barely accumulated in sperm.

references.authors: Perez-Garcia LF, Dolhain RJEM, Vorstenbosch S, et al.
references.title: The effect of paternal exposure to immunosuppressive drugs on sexual function, reproductive hormones, fertility, pregnancy and offspring outcomes: a systematic review.
references.finding: Clear negative effects on sperm for sulfasalazine and cyclophosphamide; dubious effects for methotrexate, colchicine and sirolimus; no large negative offspring effects of paternal immunosuppressants reported.

references.authors: Sammaritano LR, Bermas BL, Chakravarty EE, et al.
references.title: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Reproductive Health in Rheumatic and Musculoskeletal Diseases.
references.finding: ACR 2020 reproductive-health guideline: contraception, pre-pregnancy counselling, and continuing pregnancy-compatible medications; low-dose methotrexate may be continued in men planning conception.

references.authors: Banerjee A, Scarpa M, Pathak S, et al.
references.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease Therapies Adversely Affect Fertility in Men- A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
references.journal: Endocr Metab Immune Disord Drug Targets
references.finding: Sulphasalazine-treated men had lower sperm counts and motility and more oligospermia than mesalazine-treated men; biologics appeared safe.

references.authors: Hellstrom WJ, Sikka SC
references.title: Effects of acute treatment with tamsulosin versus alfuzosin on ejaculatory function in normal volunteers.
references.finding: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg daily lowered ejaculate volume by 2.4 mL and caused anejaculation in 35% of men; alfuzosin and placebo did not.

references.authors: Sakata K, Morita T
references.title: Investigation of ejaculatory disorder by silodosin in the treatment of prostatic hyperplasia.
references.finding: Among sexually active men on silodosin, 95% reported ejaculatory disorder.

references.authors: Girum T, Wasie A
references.title: Return of fertility after discontinuation of contraception: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: 83.1% of women conceived within 12 months of stopping contraception, with no difference between hormonal methods and IUDs or by duration of pill use.

references.authors: Yland JJ, Bresnick KA, Hatch EE, et al.
references.title: Pregravid contraceptive use and fecundability: prospective cohort study.
references.finding: Return to normal fertility took about 5-8 cycles after injectables (FR 0.65), 4 after the patch, 3 after pill or ring and 2 after IUDs or implants; total years of hormonal use did not matter.

references.authors: Lam JR, Schneider JL, Zhao W, et al.
references.title: Proton pump inhibitor and histamine 2 receptor antagonist use and vitamin B12 deficiency.
references.finding: Two or more years of PPI use was associated with 65% higher odds of B12 deficiency (OR 1.65), higher at >1.5 pills/day (OR 1.95).

references.authors: Lam JR, Schneider JL, Quesenberry CP, et al.
references.title: Proton Pump Inhibitor and Histamine-2 Receptor Antagonist Use and Iron Deficiency.
references.finding: Two or more years of PPI use was associated with iron deficiency (OR 2.49), rising with dose and falling after stopping.

references.authors: Choudhury A, Jena A, Jearth V, et al.
references.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency and use of proton pump inhibitors: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: PPI users had modestly higher odds of B12 deficiency (OR 1.42) with significant heterogeneity; most studies found no difference in serum B12 levels.

references.authors: Cheungpasitporn W, Thongprayoon C, Kittanamongkolchai W, et al.
references.title: Proton pump inhibitors linked to hypomagnesemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
references.finding: PPI use was associated with a 43% higher risk of hypomagnesemia (RR 1.43; 1.63 in high-quality studies).

references.authors: Moayyedi P, Eikelboom JW, Bosch J, et al.
references.title: Safety of Proton Pump Inhibitors Based on a Large, Multi-Year, Randomized Trial of Patients Receiving Rivaroxaban or Aspirin.
references.finding: Pantoprazole 40 mg for about 3 years caused no excess of pneumonia, fracture, dementia or other harms versus placebo except enteric infections (1.4% vs 1.0%).

references.authors: Imhann F, Bonder MJ, Vich Vila A, et al.
references.title: Proton pump inhibitors affect the gut microbiome.
references.finding: PPI use was associated with lower gut microbial diversity and changes in 20% of taxa, including more oral bacteria and potential pathogens, an effect larger than antibiotics at population level.

references.authors: Palleja A, Mikkelsen KH, Forslund SK, et al.
references.title: Recovery of gut microbiota of healthy adults following antibiotic exposure.
references.finding: After a 4-day broad-spectrum antibiotic cocktail, gut microbiota recovered to near-baseline within 1.5 months, though 9 common species were still missing at 180 days.

references.authors: Keihani S, Craig JR, Zhang C, et al.
references.title: Proton-pump inhibitor use does not affect semen quality in subfertile men.
references.n: 248 PPI users vs 7698 unmedicated subfertile men
references.finding: PPI use for over 3 months was not associated with changes in semen parameters.

references.authors: Huijgen NA, de Ridder MA, Verhamme KM, et al.
references.title: Are proton-pump inhibitors harmful for the semen quality of men in couples who are planning pregnancy?
references.finding: PPI use 6-12 months before semen analysis was associated with threefold higher odds of low total motile sperm count (OR 2.96), but use in the preceding 6 months was not.

references.authors: Ambrosone CB, Zirpoli GR, Hutson AD, et al.
references.title: Dietary Supplement Use During Chemotherapy and Survival Outcomes of Patients With Breast Cancer Enrolled in a Cooperative Group Clinical Trial (SWOG S0221).
references.n: 1134 women with breast cancer in a chemotherapy trial
references.finding: Antioxidant supplement use before and during chemotherapy was associated with higher recurrence (adjHR 1.41, CI 0.98-2.04); B12 and iron use were significantly linked to worse outcomes.

references.authors: Bairati I, Meyer F, Gélinas M, et al.
references.title: A randomized trial of antioxidant vitamins to prevent second primary cancers in head and neck cancer patients.
references.finding: Alpha-tocopherol (with beta-carotene initially) during and after radiotherapy raised second primary cancers during supplementation (HR 2.88).

references.authors: Lawenda BD, Kelly KM, Ladas EJ, et al.
references.title: Should supplemental antioxidant administration be avoided during chemotherapy and radiation therapy?
references.finding: Concluded from RCTs that supplemental antioxidants during chemotherapy and radiotherapy should be discouraged because of possible tumour protection.

references.authors: Block KI, Koch AC, Mead MN, et al.
references.title: Impact of antioxidant supplementation on chemotherapeutic efficacy: a systematic review of the evidence from randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: No trial showed reduced chemotherapy efficacy with antioxidants and many reported fewer toxicities or better survival, but trials were small and underpowered.

references.authors: Yasueda A, Urushima H, Ito T
references.title: Efficacy and Interaction of Antioxidant Supplements as Adjuvant Therapy in Cancer Treatment: A Systematic Review.
references.finding: Harm from antioxidant supplements during cancer therapy remains unclear except for smokers having radiotherapy.

references.authors: Schürks M, Glynn RJ, Rist PM, et al.
references.title: Effects of vitamin E on stroke subtypes: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
references.finding: Vitamin E raised haemorrhagic stroke risk 22% while lowering ischaemic stroke 10%; no net effect on total stroke.

references.authors: Wachira JK, Larson MK, Harris WS
references.title: n-3 Fatty acids affect haemostasis but do not increase the risk of bleeding: clinical observations and mechanistic insights.
references.finding: Omega-3 fatty acids alter platelet function but did not increase clinically significant bleeding, including with antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs.

references.authors: Javaid M, Kadhim K, Bawamia B, et al.
references.title: Bleeding Risk in Patients Receiving Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
references.finding: Omega-3 PUFAs did not increase bleeding overall (RR 1.09, 0.91-1.31); high-dose purified EPA raised relative bleeding risk about 50% but absolute risk only 0.6%.

references.authors: Tan CSS, Lee SWH
references.title: Warfarin and food, herbal or dietary supplement interactions: A systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review of warfarin interactions: 45 foods, herbs or supplements potentiated warfarin, some causing serious bleeding; St John's wort, green tea and others flagged.

references.authors: Corrigan JJ, Ulfers LL
references.title: Effect of vitamin E on prothrombin levels in warfarin-induced vitamin K deficiency.
references.finding: Vitamin E 100-400 IU/day for 4 weeks did not change prothrombin time in warfarin users, though it subtly reduced functional factor II; higher doses may potentiate vitamin K deficiency.

references.authors: Horowitz JD, Henry CA, Syrjanen ML, et al.
references.title: Combined use of nitroglycerin and N-acetylcysteine in the management of unstable angina pectoris.
references.finding: Adding IV NAC to IV nitroglycerin cut myocardial infarction (3 vs 10 patients) but caused symptomatic hypotension in 7 vs 0 patients.

references.authors: Ardissino D, Merlini PA, Savonitto S, et al.
references.title: Effect of transdermal nitroglycerin or N-acetylcysteine, or both, in the long-term treatment of unstable angina pectoris.
references.finding: Transdermal nitroglycerin plus oral NAC reduced outcome events (13% vs 39% placebo) but caused side effects, mainly intolerable headache, in 35%.

references.authors: Hall SD, Wang Z, Huang SM, et al.
references.title: The interaction between St John's wort and an oral contraceptive.
references.finding: St John's wort increased norethindrone clearance and halved ethinyl estradiol half-life; breakthrough bleeding rose from 2 to 7 of 12 women.

references.authors: Whitten DL, Myers SP, Hawrelak JA, et al.
references.title: The effect of St John's wort extracts on CYP3A: a systematic review of prospective clinical trials.
references.finding: High-hyperforin St John's wort extracts (>10 mg/day) consistently induce CYP3A; low-hyperforin extracts (<4 mg/day) did not.

references.authors: US Food and Drug Administration; Novo Nordisk
references.title: WEGOVY (semaglutide) injection, prescribing information (revised 06/2021)
references.finding: Label section 8.3: discontinue semaglutide at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy because of its long half-life; discontinue when pregnancy is recognized.

references.authors: US Food and Drug Administration; Eli Lilly
references.title: ZEPBOUND (tirzepatide) injection, prescribing information (revised 11/2023)
references.finding: A single 5 mg tirzepatide dose cut ethinyl estradiol Cmax 59% and AUC 20%; users of oral contraceptives should switch to a non-oral method or add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation.

references.authors: US Food and Drug Administration
references.title: FDA requests removal of strongest warning against using cholesterol-lowering statins during pregnancy; still advises most pregnant patients should stop taking statins (Drug Safety Communication, 20 July 2021)
references.finding: FDA removed the pregnancy contraindication for statins because observational data showed no increase in birth defects, while advising most patients to stop on learning they are pregnant, allowing continuation in very high-risk patients, and advising against breastfeeding.
